title: Five ways to turn a selection into a container
brief: Several objects are selected; one move should hold them together as a container. The same fixture is used throughout — read_frame(), detect(), annotate() and publish(), wired and multi-selected. Ground truth first, all of it driven in the running product: the containers that exist are frame, branch, branch-arm, and a Block whose view is expanded, plus stock groups. FigJam's “Wrap in new section” is not in tldraw 5.3.2 and not in this repository (0 hits in the engine, 0 in src/) — but the engine's own equivalent already ships as “Frame selection”, two levels down inside the stock Edit submenu, and it is its own inverse. Its advertised Ctrl+Alt+G was measured not to fire on this platform. Two directions were gated out during generation and are not shown: one that picked the container type by inspecting what was selected, and one that synthesised boundary ports from the cables crossing the new edge — both derive structure at conversion time, which this board does not do.
defaultWhy: Wrap Tile is the provisional choice at 92.6/100. It is the only direction that is present at the moment of intent — the control arrives with the selection rather than waiting behind a right-click or a keystroke — and it is a direct copy of the FigJam control this repository has already measured against the live FigJam editor, placed on a selection menu that already exists and already carries one-shot commands (88 lines, 2 buttons). Its broad face can call the stock frame-selection action, so the frame case stays on one code path, and the same tile flipping to Unwrap keeps the way back on the control the user just pressed.
decisionHinge: Wrap Tile leads Turn Into ▸ by 3.2 points, a hair outside co-leader range — treat it as a soft lead. The hinge is the weight on being findable at the moment of intent: move six points from that criterion into stock-seam cost and Turn Into ▸ wins 91.8 to 91.4, because a TldrawUiMenuSubmenu is a seam the same file already uses 7 times while a split control with a popover is new product code. The contested assumption is that the remembered last-used container will usually be right; if it is wrong often, the broad face becomes a trap and the menu direction is safer. Two findings apply whichever wins: the dead Ctrl+Alt+G binding should be repaired, and the duplicate pair of remove-frame commands in one context menu should collapse to one rather than gain a third.
invariants: Converting is create-container + reparent. Nothing is inferred, validated, or linted at conversion time.
Cables crossing the new boundary are left crossing it; no boundary ports are synthesised. The renderer already permits this — an Expanded Block declines to clip a connection child.
Only tldraw 5.3.2 through supported seams: menus, action overrides, registered shape utils. No engine fork.
Whatever wraps must un-wrap from the container itself.
The command reads the selection the user already made.
The container vocabulary is fixed: frame, branch, branch-arm, and a Block whose view is expanded, plus a stock group.
boundary: Exploration only — nothing under src/ was changed, and no direction is implemented. The ground truth is real: the container inventory, the menu contents, the wrap, the un-wrap and the shortcut table were all driven in the running product over CDP and are recorded in docs/assets/turn-into-ground-truth-2026-09-03.json, with the screenshots on this page taken from that same run. The five command surfaces themselves are drawn mocks over that fixture; no variant has been built, and the cost estimates are readings of the existing source rather than measured implementations.

requirements.name: Converting stays cheap, dumb and reversible
requirements.why: The board is a hackable drawing surface, not a language front end. Wrapping must move records and nothing else — no inference, no validation, no synthesised ports — and the un-wrap must be one obvious move away.
requirements.passCondition: The command's whole effect is create-container + reparent, and a single named command puts the objects back where they were.

anchors.1: Conversion reads the selection's contents to decide structure, or the inverse is a different destructive command.
anchors.3: Conversion is mechanical, but the inverse is reached somewhere unrelated to the thing that was made.
anchors.5: Conversion is create + reparent only, and the inverse sits on the container itself.

requirements.name: Borrowed muscle memory, not a new interaction
requirements.why: The standing rule is to compose from gestures a whiteboard user already owns. FigJam and tldraw are the two oracles, and both already answer this question.
requirements.passCondition: Every gesture in the direction can be pointed at in FigJam or in stock tldraw.

anchors.1: Introduces a gesture neither oracle has.
anchors.3: Uses a familiar surface but changes what a familiar control does.
anchors.5: Every step is a control or keystroke that already exists in one of the two oracles.

requirements.name: Findable at the moment of intent
requirements.why: The trigger is 'I have just selected these and want them held together'. A command that only rewards prior knowledge will not be used, however cheap it is to build.
requirements.passCondition: With a fresh multi-selection, a user who has never seen the feature can reach it.

anchors.1: Invisible: keyboard-only, or requires knowing a menu path in advance.
anchors.3: One deliberate click away, inside a menu the user already opens.
anchors.5: Visible on the selection itself, with no click spent looking.

requirements.name: Rides a stock seam already used here
requirements.why: tldraw stays stock and pinned. The cheapest safe direction is one built from a component / action / override seam this repository already composes with.
requirements.passCondition: The direction is expressible in tldraw's menu, action-override, or shape seams, with no new tool, no new gesture engine, and no fork.

anchors.1: Needs engine behaviour tldraw does not expose.
anchors.3: Fits a supported seam but adds a new subsystem beside it.
anchors.5: Is a further use of a seam already present in this tree.

requirements.name: Extends what ships instead of rivalling it
requirements.why: The engine already wraps a selection and already un-wraps it. This tree has already grown one duplicate of an engine command; a second one is a real cost, not a theoretical one.
requirements.passCondition: The frame case routes through the engine's own action rather than a parallel command.

anchors.1: Adds a second command with the same effect as a stock one, in the same menu.
anchors.3: Sits beside the stock command without contradicting it.
anchors.5: Re-registers or wraps the stock command so there is exactly one code path.

hardGates.name: Nothing is derived at conversion time
hardGates.why: No linting, no type inference, no boundary ports synthesised from the cables that cross the new edge. Cables simply cross, which the renderer already permits.

hardGates.name: Stock tldraw 5.3.2 through supported seams
hardGates.why: No engine fork and no reimplemented primitive; the stock-boundary test must stay green.

hardGates.name: Reversible by an obviously related move
hardGates.why: Whatever wraps must un-wrap from the container itself, not from an unrelated command.

hardGates.name: No invented whiteboard gesture
hardGates.why: Every gesture must already exist in FigJam or in stock tldraw.

hardGates.name: Acts on the selection the user already made
hardGates.why: The brief is 'select several things, then convert them'. A direction that discards the selection answers a different question.

variants.name: Turn Into ▸
variants.thesis: Put one top-level “Turn into ▸” submenu in the context menu the product already owns, listing the four container types, beside the detach commands that are its inverse.
variants.bestWhen: The container type genuinely varies shot to shot and the user wants to read the options before committing to one.
variants.losesWhen: The common case is one container type used over and over — then a right-click plus a hover plus a click is three moves for a decision the user had already made.

variants.name: Wrap Tile
variants.thesis: Put a split Wrap control on the floating selection menu that only exists while two or more objects are selected — broad face wraps into the last container used, chevron picks a different one.
variants.bestWhen: Wrapping is a frequent, low-ceremony act and the user usually wants the same container they used last time.
variants.losesWhen: The selection menu is already crowded, or the remembered default is wrong often enough that the broad face becomes a trap the user has to undo.

variants.name: Wrap Now, Name It Later
variants.thesis: Take the type choice out of the command entirely: one move always makes a plain Frame, and the container is retyped afterwards from its own header — the way a Block's view is already changed.
variants.bestWhen: The user does not yet know what the thing is. Wrapping is the cheap act of saying “these belong together”; the semantics arrive later, if ever.
variants.losesWhen: The user always knows the type up front — then every wrap costs a second, separate retyping step, and the board briefly fills with frames nobody meant.

decisions.label: Type choice
decisions.value: Deferred to a Turn into ▸ on the container's own menu, read off the visible object.

decisions.label: Lowering
decisions.value: Frame → Block/Branch reparents the same children and carries the name across.

decisions.label: Inverse
decisions.value: Remove frame, which the engine already offers for every frame-like shape.

proof: Retyping-from-the-object is an idiom this product already has: a Block's view is changed from its own context menu across 4 values (simple, port, expanded, value).
The un-wrap is already engine-provided for whatever it becomes: Remove frame is offered for any frame-like shape, and in this tree that means BlockShapeUtil, BranchArmShapeUtil, BranchShapeUtil.
Driven in the running product: clicking Remove frame on the wrapped frame left all four objects loose and selected (4 of 4, 0 frames remaining).

fr1.evidence: This is the dumbest possible conversion — one act, no branch, and the engine's own Remove frame is the inverse.

fr2.evidence: Retyping off an object's header is a familiar move here, but 'wrap first, decide later' is not something either oracle does; both pick the container up front.

fr3.evidence: The wrap itself is a single visible move, but the retype is a second thing to discover on a second object.

fr4.evidence: The wrap is stock, but lowering an existing frame into a Block or Branch while keeping children and name is new machinery with no stock equivalent.

fr5.evidence: The wrap is literally the stock frame-selection action, unmodified.

g2.evidence: The wrap is a stock action; the retype is a shape-level command in a registered shape util.

g3.evidence: Remove frame sits on the container and works for every frame-like shape in this tree.

g4.evidence: No gesture at all — a menu item and a keystroke.

g5.evidence: frame-selection operates on the current selection.

variants.name: Same Key Family
variants.thesis: Add no surface at all: repair the stock frame-selection shortcut, which this build advertises and does not fire, and give it two siblings so the container type is the key you press.
variants.bestWhen: The user already lives in Ctrl+G / Ctrl+Shift+G and wants the fourth and fifth members of a family they can feel rather than read.
variants.losesWhen: Anyone has to be told the feature exists — which, on a board whose menu currently lies about the binding, is everyone.

decisions.value: None. TLUiOverrides.actions only.

decisions.label: Type choice
decisions.value: The key: G frame, B block, R branch — no picker exists.

decisions.label: Repair
decisions.value: frame-selection ships kbd 'cmd+alt+g' with no ctrl alternative, unlike group's 'cmd+g,ctrl+g'.

decisions.label: Inverse
decisions.value: The same keystroke again — frame-selection already routes an all-frames selection to removeFrame.

keepParts: fixing the dead ctrl binding regardless of which direction wins
keeping the frame case on the engine's own action
proof: Measured in the running product with the canvas focused by a real click (docs/turn_into_probe.mjs): Ctrl+G grouped (groups 0 -> 1), Ctrl+Shift+G ungrouped (groups 1 -> 0), and Ctrl+Alt+G — the binding the menu prints — did nothing (frames 0 -> 0).
Meta+Alt+G, the literal kbd string the engine registers, did fire: frames 0 -> 1, and pressing it again put the objects back (frames 1 -> 0). So the label is right and the binding is not.

The cause is in the pinned engine's action table: frame-selection carries kbd 'cmd+alt+g' while group carries 'cmd+g,ctrl+g' and ungroup 'cmd+shift+g,ctrl+shift+g' — the ctrl alternative is simply missing.

fr1.evidence: A keystroke that runs the stock action is the least ceremony possible, and the same keystroke is the documented inverse.

fr2.evidence: Ctrl+G / Ctrl+Shift+G is deep muscle memory, but Ctrl+Alt+B and Ctrl+Alt+R are invented members of the family.

fr3.evidence: Nothing appears anywhere. Worse than invisible today, because the one label that does exist prints a binding that was measured not to fire.

fr4.evidence: TLUiOverrides is already how this tree reshapes the toolbar; re-registering an action id is the same seam.

fr5.evidence: It is the stock command, re-registered with a working binding — one code path, not two.

g2.evidence: Action overrides are a documented tldraw seam already used in toolbarIntegration.ts.

g3.evidence: Measured: the second press of the same chord took the frame back off (frames 1 -> 0).

g5.evidence: canApplySelectionAction gates the stock action on the live selection.

variants.name: Draw It Over Them
variants.thesis: Do not put a command on the selection at all: pick the container on the tool belt where it already lives, drag a box around the objects, and the box adopts what it encloses.
variants.bestWhen: The user is composing rather than reorganising — the boundary is the thing they want to place, and the contents follow from where they drew it.
variants.losesWhen: They have already made the selection. Every marquee, shift-click and lasso is thrown away, and an awkward or non-rectangular selection cannot be re-enclosed at all.

proof: The container tools are already on the belt: the toolbar exposes a Frame tile plus a system family of block, branch and pill.
tldraw's frame tool already adopts the shapes it is drawn over, so the frame case needs no product code at all.
It cannot answer the brief as asked: the probe's four-object selection is discarded, and the user must draw a rectangle that happens to enclose exactly those four.

fr1.evidence: Mechanical, but 'enclosed' is an implicit rule the user has to learn, and a near-miss silently leaves an object out.

fr2.evidence: Drawing a frame over shapes is stock tldraw, and drawing a FigJam section over objects behaves the same way.

fr3.evidence: The tool belt is permanently visible, but nothing about a live selection suggests this is the way to hold it together.

fr4.evidence: Free for frames; extending adoption to Block and Branch changes the create behaviour of two registered tools.

fr5.evidence: It is a parallel route to the same outcome that neither uses nor replaces the stock selection action.

g1.evidence: Membership comes from geometry the user drew, not from anything read off the contents.

g2.evidence: The frame case is entirely stock; the others are shape-util create seams.

g3.evidence: Remove frame works on the drawn container, as on any frame-like shape.

g4.evidence: Drag-to-create is the most stock gesture there is.

g5.evidence: It discards the selection entirely. The user's marquee, shift-clicks and lasso are thrown away and the boundary must be re-drawn by hand, which a non-rectangular selection cannot express at all.
